Transcript Body:
[00:00] Sarah Kim: Hi everyone thanks for joining, quick intros and then Ravi will walk through the long context perf approach.
[00:18] Dr. Elena Morales: Hi all, from MedTech, we're trying to keep de-identified patient histories across entire care episodes — that's routinely 50k to 200k tokens, so 128k is our first target. Latency target is sub-3s for incremental queries, overall batch processing can be higher.
[00:42] Sarah Kim: Got it. Ravi do you want to start with the KV cache and chunking patterns?
[00:50] Ravi Patel: Sure. High-level: when you go past typical 32k sequences you need a different memory and attention strategy. Two axes — how you feed the context into the attention (chunking / sliding window / global tokens) and how you persist KV state across requests. For MedTech the best pattern we see is a hybrid: persistent prefix KV caching plus chunked on-demand retrieval.
[01:20] Jamal Reed: Can you explain persistent prefix KV caching — does that keep full keys in GPU memory? We're worried about OOM.
[01:29] Ravi Patel: Good question. We keep the most recent and highest-value KV entries in HBM, and evict/roll to NVMe for cold chunks. So at runtime the engine can stream KV pages from NVMe with prefetching to HBM. It's not all-in-memory; we expose eviction policies and checkpointing. That allows a ~128k working set without requiring multi-TB HBM.
[01:58] Priya Singh: How does that affect tail latency for single-query incremental reads — we need sub-3s 95th.
[02:07] Ravi Patel: Prefetching is key. For incremental queries we do prefix-only KV retrieval from HBM for the near context, then async fetch for older chunks. For strict SLOs we can pin high-frequency patient contexts to dedicated HBM (Dedicated pool) or use a hot-cache in memory (memory-resident KV). For cold traces you pay the NVMe hop which adds ~200-400ms depending on PCIe and NVMe tier.
[02:40] Dr. Elena Morales: Are there kernel/attention changes needed? We looked at FlashAttention and grouped query approaches.
[02:49] Ravi Patel: Yes FlashAttention or memory-efficient attention kernels are standard for long context. We also support block-sparse and grouped-query attention variants where global tokens attend across chunks. Practically, we chunk into overlapping windows (e.g., 8k windows with 1k overlap) and use a lightweight global index embedding so cross-chunk references are cheap. This reduces quadratic blowup.
[03:20] Jamal Reed: Overlaps increase compute though — how do you balance throughput?
[03:27] Ravi Patel: Right. There's a tradeoff: smaller windows -> less per-window quadratic cost but more windows overall. We recommend adaptive chunking driven by semantic boundaries: variable-length chunking using sentence/segment detectors reduces unnecessary overlap. Also continuous batching helps — we batch many queries against the same chunk set to amortize the attention cost.
[03:52] Sarah Kim: On batching — customer wanted near real-time incremental queries. How do you avoid increased latency with batching?
[03:59] Ravi Patel: We do micro-batching: small, time-bounded batches (20-50ms collect window) for live traffic to enable some batching efficiency but keep latency low. For throughput jobs/ingestion you batch bigger. We also have shaped routing: route latency-sensitive requests to lower-batch, higher-cost nodes.
[04:22] Priya Singh: Quantization — we saw artifacts with 4-bit in our tests. What's Redwood's recommendation for safety/quality in clinical context?
[04:30] Ravi Patel: For clinical workloads we advise starting with 8-bit or 4-bit-but-calibrated with per-layer scaling and selective fp16 for sensitive layers. We provide regression tests and eval harnesses — if you quantize to 4-bit you should run the prompt eval suite (we'll share the harness). Also consider model surgicalization: keep attention/query projection layers at higher precision.
[04:58] Dr. Elena Morales: How about model sharding vs tensor parallelism for 128k?
[05:04] Ravi Patel: Model sharding across GPUs helps with memory but increases cross-GPU comms during attention. We often combine operator-level partitioning with KV sharding: keep KV for active chunks local to the GPU serving that tenant and use NCCL-optimized all-reduce for smaller synchronization. For latency-sensitive single-tenant deployments Dedicated or Private on-prem gives the most predictable performance because you can avoid noisy neighbors and tailor HBM/NVMe configs.
[05:36] Jamal Reed: Any rule-of-thumb for GPUs and HBM for 128k context?
[05:41] Ravi Patel: Roughly speaking, 128k of tokens with 32-byte KV per token is ~4MB per token? Wait that's off — let me recalc verbally — the KV per token depends on hidden size, but practical numbers: a 70B model might need dozens of GBs of KV. In practice we recommend configurations with >=80GB HBM per instance (A100-80GB or H100 equivalents) and NVMe for overflow. For cost-conscious setups, multi-node with NVMe offload is common. We'll include sizing tables in the benchmark doc.
[06:18] Sarah Kim: Let's talk security and on-prem. They require SOC2 plus customer-managed KMS and strict egress.
[06:26] Dr. Elena Morales: Yes we cannot have any PHI egress. Prefer on-prem with HSM or VPC private endpoints — audit logs are mandatory.
[06:35] Sarah Kim: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and audit logs, and our Private control plane can be configured to avoid internet egress. We'll share the SOC2 and HSM integration notes.
[06:46] Ravi Patel: For on-prem, the big work is network topology and NVMe visibility from GPU hosts. We usually run a small bench to validate PCIe lanes and NVMe throughput; if it's suboptimal we recommend local NVMe or using NVMe-oF.
[07:05] Jamal Reed: About benchmarking — can you share the exact scripts and metrics you run? We want to reproduce.
[07:12] Ravi Patel: Yes we've got a public runbook; I'll upload the harness and configs. Typical metrics: end-to-end latency (P50/P95/P99), tokens/sec, GPU utilization, HBM occupancy, NVMe IOPs, and memory page faults. We'll include trace-level logs so you can spot KV fetch stalls.
[07:33] Priya Singh: For the eval suite, will you run QA on clinical prompts? We will provide de-identified examples.
[07:40] Ravi Patel: Absolutely. We'll run the evals in a sandbox using your de-identified set. We'll compare quality across fp16/8-bit/4-bit and provide per-prompt deltas.
[07:51] Dr. Elena Morales: Can we try the Dedicated pool first? We want to test 2 nodes for a pilot.
[07:57] Sarah Kim: Sounds good; Sarah to share pricing and a 30-day pilot contract option.
[08:04] Jamal Reed: About failure modes — if a KV page fails to load mid-query what's the graceful fallback?
[08:12] Ravi Patel: We have automatic fallback policies: degrade to shorter context summarization (summarize older chunks into embeddings stored in a compact index), or route to a compatible smaller model. You can set policy to fail-safe-mode which returns a deterministic summary with an indication it omitted older context.
[08:34] Priya Singh: Any concern with PCIe bandwidth on our current hosts (mix of older Gen3 servers)?
[08:40] Ravi Patel: Gen3 NVMe limits will impact cold fetch times. We recommend validating NVMe bandwidth with our microbench; if insufficient, use local NVMe on GPU hosts or upgrade to Gen4. We can run a quick benchmark during the on-prem workshop.
[09:00] Sarah Kim: Quick recap before we close?
[09:05] Ravi Patel: Recap — hybrid KV caching (HBM hot + NVMe cold), adaptive chunking with overlapping windows + global tokens, micro-batching for low-latency, selective quantization with eval harness, prefer Dedicated/Private for consistent SLOs, and run bench to size hardware.
[09:28] Dr. Elena Morales: Good. We'll get the prompt set and infra diagram.
[09:33] Sarah Kim: Great. I'll send pricing and contract options. Ravi will send the benchmark runbook.
[09:38] Jamal Reed: Thanks everyone.
[09:40] End of call.
